oxabolone.summary: A nandrolone-family anabolic steroid that users associate with lean mass gain; it is banned in sport and little has been published on it.

quick.overview:
Oxabolone is an anabolic steroid in the nandrolone family. People who discuss it in muscle-building circles associate it with lean mass gain and a fuller, more muscular physique.

As an anabolic-androgenic steroid it is classed as an androgen receptor agonist, the signalling that drives greater muscle protein synthesis. The parent compound was never sold as a drug, though an injectable ester, oxabolone cipionate, has seen medical use. Almost nothing has been published on it, and no trials of its effects on muscle or appearance were found.
quick.how: In physique discussions it is treated as one of the lesser-known compounds in the nandrolone class, used within muscle-gain phases alongside heavy training and a calorie surplus. Specific routines are not well documented in published sources.
quick.risks: Oxabolone is on the WADA prohibited list, so it is banned in most major sports. A 1995 case report described mucosal hyperpigmentation associated with it, and no broader safety data have been published. Anabolic steroids as a class are controlled substances in many countries.

angle.text: Oxabolone is a nandrolone-family anabolic steroid that users associate with lean mass gain. The route is anabolic steroid signalling, which drives greater muscle protein synthesis and more muscle mass. Very little has been published on it specifically.

sm-130686.summary: An experimental oral growth hormone secretagogue that works through the ghrelin receptor, discussed for leaner, fuller-looking physiques.

quick.overview:
SM-130686 is an oral compound that stimulates growth hormone release, and it gets mentioned in muscle and anti-aging circles because higher growth hormone is linked to a leaner, fuller-looking physique.

It activates the ghrelin (growth hormone secretagogue) receptor, which triggers growth hormone release from pituitary cells in laboratory studies. Unlike peptide secretagogues it is a small molecule designed to work by mouth. The published literature is chemistry and animal or cell pharmacology from the 2000s; no human trials have been reported.
quick.how: It is not an approved medicine, and there is no established routine for it. In discussions it is grouped with other growth hormone secretagogues that people pair with training and sleep, aiming at body composition changes over months.
quick.risks: Human safety has not been published, and the compound is experimental. Secretagogues are detectable in urine, and analytical methods for doping control exist.

angle.text: SM-130686 is an oral growth hormone secretagogue mentioned in muscle and anti-aging circles. It activates the ghrelin receptor to raise growth hormone release, which is linked to a leaner, more muscular look. It is known from lab and animal papers.

bezafibrate.summary: A prescription lipid drug that activates PPAR receptors, discussed in fat-loss circles alongside PPAR-delta compounds for a leaner body.

quick.overview:
Bezafibrate is a long-established prescription drug for high triglycerides and mixed cholesterol problems. It comes up in fat-loss conversations because it activates the PPAR family of receptors, including PPAR-delta, the pathway behind compounds like GW501516 and linked to greater fat burning and a leaner body.

It acts mainly on PPAR-alpha, with some activity at PPAR-gamma and PPAR-delta, increasing triglyceride breakdown and altering HDL metabolism. Its trial record is in cardiovascular disease, dyslipidemia and the liver condition primary biliary cholangitis; no trials of fat loss or appearance outcomes were found.
quick.how: Its documented use is a prescribed oral tablet for blood lipids, taken under a doctor's supervision. In fat-loss forums posters mention it as a related PPAR option during cutting phases, alongside diet and training.
quick.risks: Reported effects include abnormal liver enzymes, muscle problems (rarely severe) and gastrointestinal upset. Sources list it as contraindicated in severe liver or kidney impairment, gallstone disease and pregnancy. It is prescription-only.

angle.text: Bezafibrate is a lipid-lowering drug that acts on PPAR receptors, including the PPAR-delta pathway linked to greater fat burning and a leaner body composition. Fat-loss forums mention it as a relative of GW501516-type compounds. Its documented studies concern blood lipids and liver disease.

seladelpar.summary: An FDA-approved PPAR-delta agonist for a liver condition, followed in fat-loss circles because it hits the same target as GW501516.

quick.overview:
Seladelpar is a prescription PPAR-delta agonist approved in the US in 2024 for primary biliary cholangitis, a chronic liver disease. Fat-loss circles follow it because PPAR-delta is the same receptor targeted by GW501516-type compounds, which are promoted for endurance, greater fat burning and leanness.

It activates PPAR-delta, which reduces bile acid synthesis in liver cells; the label says the precise mechanism in PBC is not well understood. Its trials measure liver markers and itch, not fat loss or looks.
quick.how: Its documented use is a once-daily prescription for adults with PBC, taken with ursodeoxycholic acid or alone if that is not tolerated. Use for body composition is discussed online but is outside its approved purpose.
quick.risks: Reported adverse reactions include headache, abdominal pain, nausea, abdominal distension and dizziness. The label warns about fractures, liver test abnormalities and biliary obstruction. It is available by prescription only.

angle.text: Seladelpar is an approved PPAR-delta agonist that fat-loss circles watch because PPAR-delta activation is linked to greater fat burning and a leaner body. Its approved studies concern liver disease, not body composition.

elafibranor.summary: An approved dual PPAR-alpha/delta agonist for a liver condition, mentioned in fat-loss talk because PPAR-delta is linked to fat burning.

quick.overview:
Elafibranor is a prescription drug approved in 2024 for primary biliary cholangitis. It activates two PPAR receptors, alpha and delta, and PPAR-delta activation is the link fat-loss circles draw to greater fat metabolism and a leaner body.

It and its main metabolite activate PPAR-alpha and PPAR-delta (and PPAR-gamma in vitro), receptors that regulate fat and bile acid metabolism. It was earlier developed for NASH, where a large phase 3 trial was terminated. Its trials track liver markers; none examine body composition or looks.
quick.how: Its documented use is a daily oral prescription for adults with PBC, with ursodeoxycholic acid or alone. Fat-loss use is discussed online but is outside its approved purpose.
quick.risks: Reported reactions include weight gain, diarrhea, abdominal pain, nausea, joint pain, muscle injury and fracture, among others. It is prescription-only.

angle.text: Elafibranor is an approved dual PPAR-alpha/delta agonist. PPAR-delta activation is linked to greater fat metabolism and a leaner body, which is why it appears in fat-loss discussion. Its trials concern liver disease.

gw0742.summary: A PPAR-delta research compound sold gray-market as 'Cardarine 2.0', taken in cutting phases for fat burning and endurance.

quick.overview:
GW0742 is a selective PPAR-delta agonist made by GlaxoSmithKline and used mostly as a lab tool. Bodybuilding and fat-loss communities market it as a stronger sibling of GW501516, and users take it in cutting phases hoping for greater fat burning, endurance and a leaner, more defined physique.

It activates PPAR-delta, a nuclear receptor involved in fatty acid oxidation, glucose handling and inflammation. Published research is cell and animal work on inflammation, metabolism and the heart; no human trials were found.
quick.how: It is sold gray-market as a research chemical, usually in oral form, and users pair it with a calorie deficit and cardio during cutting phases. Typical run lengths and results are reported only anecdotally.
quick.risks: It is not an approved medicine and human safety data are lacking. Rodent studies of the related GW501516 reported tumour promotion, and that concern is cited for GW0742 as well. Use in sport is a concern for athletes subject to testing.

angle.text: GW0742 is a research PPAR-delta agonist that users take in cutting phases hoping for greater fat oxidation, endurance and a more defined physique. The research behind it is lab and animal data.

l-165041.summary: A lab PPAR-delta agonist from the GW501516 family, studied in cells and mice for how it shifts fat metabolism.

quick.overview:
L-165041 is a laboratory compound that switches on PPAR-delta, a receptor that helps control how cells handle fats. It appears in fat-loss and endurance discussions as another member of the GW501516 family, with users linking the pathway to greater fat burning and leanness.

It binds PPAR-delta, which regulates genes involved in fatty acid metabolism. In insulin-resistant db/db mice it altered lipid metabolism, and in cultured rat heart cells it reduced hypertrophic responses. It has not been tested in people for fat loss.
quick.how: It is listed by chemical suppliers as a research tool and is used in lab experiments. Online it is discussed as an alternative to better-known PPAR-delta compounds, with no established routine.
quick.risks: No human safety data exist. It is a research chemical and not an approved medicine.

angle.text: L-165041 is a lab PPAR-delta agonist discussed as part of the GW501516 family, with users linking the pathway to greater fat burning and leanness. Evidence comes from cell and mouse studies.

acadesine.summary: An AMPK activator marketed as an exercise mimetic for fat burning and endurance without extra training.

quick.overview:
Acadesine (AICAR) activates AMPK, a cellular energy sensor, and is promoted in fat-loss and performance circles as an exercise mimetic, with users hoping for greater fat burning and endurance without extra training.

Inside cells it is converted to an AMP-like molecule that activates AMPK, raising fat oxidation and glucose uptake in muscle in animal studies. A 2008 mouse study reported endurance gains. In humans it was tested for heart-surgery protection and some blood cancers, not fat loss, and the surgery trial stopped for futility.
quick.how: It is sold online as a research compound, and users add it alongside training and dieting in cutting phases. Reported routines are anecdotal, and no human body-composition protocol has been published.
quick.risks: It is not approved for body-composition use, and it has been on the WADA prohibited list since 2009. Human safety data for that use are lacking.

angle.text: Acadesine (AICAR) is promoted as an exercise mimetic: it activates AMPK, which raises fat oxidation in muscle in animal studies, and users hope for a leaner look without extra training. The idea comes from a 2008 mouse study.

slu-pp-332.summary: An experimental ERR agonist billed as an exercise mimetic, with mouse results for endurance and less fat gain.

quick.overview:
SLU-PP-332 is an experimental compound billed in fat-loss circles as an exercise mimetic that could deliver leanness and endurance gains without extra training. In mice it produced an exercise-like gene program, better running capacity and less fat gain.

It activates estrogen-related receptors alpha, beta and gamma, which control mitochondrial and fat metabolism in muscle. Published studies are in mice and cells, including models of metabolic syndrome, heart failure and kidney aging; no human results are published.
quick.how: It circulates as a research compound, and users talk about adding it to cutting phases alongside training. No human routines or timelines have been established.
quick.risks: Human safety is unknown, and it is not an approved drug. Anti-doping laboratories have published methods for detecting it.

angle.text: SLU-PP-332 is billed as an exercise mimetic: it activates estrogen-related receptors, triggering an exercise-like gene program and less fat gain in mice, and users hope for leanness and endurance without extra training.

bam-15.summary: A mitochondrial uncoupler that burns more calories as heat and cut fat in mice, discussed online as a 'safer DNP'.

quick.overview:
BAM15 is an experimental compound that makes mitochondria burn fuel as heat, and users hope it raises calorie burn and sheds fat for a leaner look. It is traded online as a 'safer DNP'.

It carries protons across the mitochondrial membrane, uncoupling food oxidation from ATP production and raising energy expenditure. In a 2014 screen it was identified as an uncoupler that did not depolarize the plasma membrane, and in mice on a high-fat diet it reduced body fat and improved insulin sensitivity without changing food intake. No human trials have been published.
quick.how: It is sold as a research chemical, and forum users discuss it as an alternative to DNP during cutting phases. No human routines have been validated.
quick.risks: Human safety is unstudied. Uncouplers as a class can cause overheating, and DNP has been linked to fatal poisonings. BAM15 is not approved.

angle.text: BAM15 is a mitochondrial uncoupler that lets cells burn more calories as heat, which users hope will lower body fat for a leaner look. In mice it reduced body fat on a high-fat diet.

adipotide.summary: An experimental peptide that targets the blood vessels feeding fat tissue; it cut weight in monkeys and development stopped.

quick.overview:
Adipotide is an experimental peptide designed to cut off the blood supply of white fat so the fat tissue shrinks, for a lower body fat and leaner look. Obese rhesus monkeys lost weight and improved insulin resistance in a 2011 study.

It binds prohibitin on fat blood vessels and triggers cell death in them. A 2012 comment proposed that reduced eating could explain part of the weight loss. No human results exist.
quick.how: It is discussed in fat-loss forums as a peptide, but it has no established human routine. Clinical development was reported discontinued as of 2019.
quick.risks: Human safety is unknown, and it is not approved.

angle.text: Adipotide is discussed as a peptide that targets the blood vessels feeding fat tissue so it shrinks, for a leaner look. Weight loss was shown in obese monkeys; development has stopped.

fenfluramine.summary: A former prescription appetite suppressant, best known in fen-phen, withdrawn in 1997 and now a restricted epilepsy medicine.

quick.overview:
Fenfluramine was a widely prescribed appetite suppressant, best known in the fen-phen combination with phentermine, and it is cited in diet-drug history as a strong weight-loss option. It reduced appetite, lowering calorie intake for a leaner body.

It releases serotonin and acts at 5-HT2 receptors, which reduces appetite. Introduced in France in 1963 and approved in the US in 1973, it was withdrawn from the US market in 1997 after reports of heart valve disease and pulmonary hypertension. A low-dose form, Fintepla, is now approved for Dravet and Lennox-Gastaut seizures, not weight loss.
quick.how: Historically it was taken as a prescription pill, often with phentermine, as a weight-loss aid. Today its only approved use is for childhood epilepsy under a restricted program.
quick.risks: The label carries a boxed warning for valvular heart disease and pulmonary arterial hypertension, and use requires echocardiogram monitoring through a restricted program.

angle.text: Fenfluramine was a prescription appetite suppressant: serotonin release reduced appetite, lowering calorie intake for a leaner body, and its weight-loss effect was studied in trials. It was withdrawn in 1997 and is now an epilepsy medicine.

ephedrine-caffeine-eca-stack.summary: A classic ephedrine, caffeine and aspirin cutting stack used for energy and appetite control while dieting down for a leaner look.

quick.overview:
ECA combines ephedrine, caffeine and aspirin. Bodybuilding and physique communities use it as a cutting aid for appetite suppression and energy while dieting for a leaner, more defined look.

Ephedrine is a sympathomimetic stimulant that raises metabolic rate and suppresses appetite, and caffeine has been reported to act synergistically with it. A 2021 systematic review summarized on Wikipedia reported about 2 kg more weight loss than placebo over roughly 4 to 24 weeks, with no statistically significant blood pressure difference in that review.
quick.how: Users take it as an oral stack during cutting phases, paired with diet and exercise. Guides on looksmax.org frame it as a cutting aid and caution against it for people with heart problems.
quick.risks: Reported effects include insomnia, anxiety, high blood pressure, fast heart rate, stroke and heart attack. The FDA banned ephedrine-alkaloid dietary supplements in 2004, and legal status varies elsewhere.

angle.text: The ECA stack is a classic cutting aid: a stimulant raises energy and suppresses appetite, helping people dieting toward a leaner, more defined physique. Trials have found modest fat-loss effects, mostly alongside diet and exercise.

zenagamtide.summary: Novo Nordisk's investigational GLP-1 plus amylin dual agonist (amycretin), with large weight loss reported in early trials.

quick.overview:
Zenagamtide, better known as amycretin, is a single molecule that activates GLP-1 and amylin receptors to lower appetite and increase fullness, leading to major weight loss and a leaner body. Novo Nordisk is developing weekly injectable and daily oral forms for obesity and diabetes.

It acts on appetite, satiety and gastric emptying. In a phase 1b/2a trial of 125 adults with overweight or obesity running up to 36 weeks, Grokipedia, an AI-generated source, reports a mean weight loss of 24.3 percent at the highest weekly dose. Early trials were published in the Lancet in 2025, and phase 3 programs were reported planned or starting.
quick.how: It is not available outside trials. In development it is given as a once-weekly injection or a daily pill, and weight change builds over months of treatment.
quick.risks: Gastrointestinal effects were the most common reported adverse events. It is investigational and not approved.

angle.text: Zenagamtide (amycretin) activates GLP-1 and amylin receptors, lowering appetite and raising fullness for major weight loss and a leaner body. Early obesity trials reported large weight-loss figures; it is not yet approved.

enicepatide.summary: Roche's weekly GLP-1/GIP dual agonist for weight loss, now in phase 3 and headed for a tirzepatide head-to-head.

quick.overview:
Enicepatide is a weekly injectable from Roche that activates GLP-1 and GIP receptors to lower appetite and drive weight loss for a leaner body. Weight-loss followers watch it as a possible rival to tirzepatide.

It is described as signal-biased, with minimal beta-arrestin coupling at either receptor. Wikipedia cites 18.8 percent placebo-adjusted weight loss at 24 weeks in a trial. Phase 3 trials are registered in obesity, with and without type 2 diabetes, including a comparison with tirzepatide.
quick.how: It is not available outside trials. In development it is a once-weekly injection for people with obesity or type 2 diabetes.
quick.risks: It is investigational and unapproved, and published safety information is limited in available sources.

angle.text: Enicepatide is Roche's weekly GLP-1/GIP dual agonist: it lowers appetite, leading to weight loss and a leaner body. It is in phase 3 trials for obesity, including a comparison with tirzepatide.

ct-996.summary: Roche's experimental oral GLP-1 pill for weight loss, with registered phase 2 trials and no results published yet.

quick.overview:
CT-996 (tifeglipron) is an experimental oral GLP-1 agonist from Roche for obesity and type 2 diabetes. Fat-loss communities follow it as a non-injectable alternative to semaglutide-type drugs, with lower appetite leading to weight loss and a leaner body.

It is a small molecule taken by mouth, rather than a peptide injection, and small-molecule oral GLP-1 drugs are designed to avoid the injection requirement. Evidence so far consists of clinical trial registrations covering phase 1 and phase 2 studies; published results were not found.
quick.how: It is not available outside trials. In development it is a pill for people with obesity or type 2 diabetes.
quick.risks: No published safety data were found, and it is not approved.

angle.text: CT-996 is an experimental oral GLP-1 pill that activates the same appetite pathway as semaglutide-type drugs, lowering appetite for weight loss and a leaner body without injections. It has registered phase 2 trials and no published results yet.

petrelintide.summary: A weekly amylin-analogue obesity drug from Zealand and Roche that increases fullness for weight loss, now in phase 3.

quick.overview:
Petrelintide is a weekly injectable amylin analogue from Zealand Pharma, partnered with Roche. It mimics amylin, a hormone that signals fullness after meals, so people feel full sooner and eat less, leading to weight loss and a leaner body.

It targets satiety rather than GLP-1 pathways and is discussed in fat-loss circles as part of the next wave of obesity drugs beyond GLP-1. A phase 1b trial reported 8.6 percent weight loss over 16 weeks, a phase 2 trial (ZUPREME 1) has been published in The Lancet Diabetes & Endocrinology, and phase 3 trials have begun recruiting. Roche is also co-developing it in combination with enicepatide.
quick.how: It is not available outside trials. In development it is a once-weekly injection for weight management.
quick.risks: Safety data come from phase 1 and 2 publications. It is investigational and not approved.

angle.text: Petrelintide is a weekly amylin analogue: it mimics a fullness hormone, lowering appetite for weight loss and a leaner body. It is in phase 3 for weight management.

eloralintide.summary: Lilly's weekly amylin agonist, with roughly 9 to 20 percent weight loss reported at 48 weeks in phase 2.

quick.overview:
Eloralintide is a weekly injectable amylin agonist from Eli Lilly. It selectively activates the amylin receptor, promoting fullness and slowing stomach emptying, which lowers appetite and drives weight loss for a leaner body.

A 48-week phase 2 trial in adults with obesity or overweight and a comorbidity was published in The Lancet in 2025. Grokipedia, an AI-generated source, reports weight loss from 9.5 percent at the lowest dose to 20.1 percent at the highest, versus 0.4 percent with placebo. Lilly began phase 3 trials in December 2025.
quick.how: It is not available outside trials. In development it is a once-weekly injection, with weight loss building over the 48-week trial period.
quick.risks: Nausea and other gastrointestinal effects were the most common adverse events. It is investigational and not approved.

angle.text: Eloralintide is Lilly's weekly amylin agonist: it increases fullness and lowers appetite, leading to weight loss and a leaner body. Phase 2 trials reported roughly 9 to 20 percent weight loss at 48 weeks.

maridebart-cafraglutide.summary: Amgen's monthly GLP-1 agonist / GIP-blocker injection, in phase 3, with roughly 12-16% weight loss at a year in phase 2.

quick.overview:
Maridebart cafraglutide (MariTide) is an experimental injectable obesity drug from Amgen, designed to be given monthly or less often rather than weekly like semaglutide or tirzepatide. It lowers appetite for weight loss and a leaner body.

It pairs an antibody that blocks the GIP receptor with GLP-1 peptides that activate the GLP-1 receptor, and the antibody backbone extends its time in the body. In a phase 2 trial of 592 adults published in the New England Journal of Medicine, average weight loss at 52 weeks was 12.3% to 16.2% in people with obesity, versus 2.5% on placebo. Large phase 3 trials (the MARITIME programme) are under way.
quick.how: It is available only inside clinical trials, given as a subcutaneous injection every 4 weeks or less often. Gradual dose escalation was used in trials to ease side effects.
quick.risks: Nausea, vomiting and other gastrointestinal events were common in phase 2, and less frequent with gradual dose escalation. No unexpected safety signals were reported. It is not approved anywhere, and long-term safety data are still being collected.

angle.text: MariTide is Amgen's monthly injection that activates GLP-1 and blocks GIP, lowering appetite for weight loss and a leaner body. Phase 2 showed roughly 12-16% weight loss at a year; it is now in phase 3.

aleniglipron.summary: An experimental once-daily GLP-1 pill that cut weight by about 8-11% (placebo-adjusted) over 36 weeks in phase 2b.

quick.overview:
Aleniglipron is an experimental once-daily oral GLP-1 agonist for obesity. It is a small-molecule pill rather than an injectable peptide, so fat-loss followers watch it as a non-injectable option for lower appetite, weight loss and a leaner body.

It activates the GLP-1 receptor, the pathway used by semaglutide and similar drugs that reduces appetite and food intake. In the 36-week ACCESS phase 2b trial of 230 adults, placebo-adjusted weight loss was 8.2%, 9.8% and 11.3% across three dose arms. Phase 3 trials (ACCOMPLISH-1 and -2) began in 2026.
quick.how: It is available only in clinical trials, taken as a once-daily pill. Weight change built over the 36 weeks of the phase 2b trial.
quick.risks: Gastrointestinal events were the main adverse effects and were mostly mild to moderate; 10.4% of drug-arm participants stopped treatment for treatment-related reasons, and no drug-induced liver injury was reported. It is not approved and long-term data are lacking.

angle.text: Aleniglipron is an experimental once-daily GLP-1 pill: it lowers appetite for weight loss and a leaner body without injections. Phase 2b showed about 8-11% placebo-adjusted weight loss over 36 weeks; phase 3 is under way.
